statement: As described in a narrative review (Angarita et al., 2016; figures second-hand, no systematic search or appraisal), alcohol helps healthy people fall asleep, but in people with alcohol use disorder sleep is disturbed during drinking and for a long time after stopping: cited studies found clinical insomnia in 35 to 70% of people with the disorder against about 15 to 30% of the general population; longer time to fall asleep and shorter sleep during drinking and through the first weeks and months of abstinence; less deep (slow-wave) sleep that may take months to years to recover; a rebound of REM (dreaming) sleep after stopping, though findings conflict; and broken sleep from the first nights of abstinence to a year or more. Self-reported insomnia early in abstinence predicted relapse in several studies, and a long time to fall asleep did in two of three, with mixed results for other sleep measures. The review's own summary table marks the early-abstinence changes for alcohol as uncertain. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: A review of sleep research says alcohol can help you fall asleep at first, but people who drink heavily for a long time sleep badly, and their sleep can stay poor for months after they stop. Bad sleep after stopping was linked with starting to drink again. These are second-hand findings from a review that did not check study quality.
population: People with alcohol use disorder in studies cited by a narrative review; healthy people for the acute effect
exposure: Regular heavy drinking and abstinence after it
comparator: Healthy sleepers, the general population, or the same people at other times, as in the cited studies
outcome: Insomnia, sleep latency, total sleep, slow-wave and REM sleep, sleep fragmentation, relapse
magnitude: Second-hand, as summarized: clinical insomnia 35 to 70% in alcohol use disorder against about 15 to 30% in the general population; reduced total sleep at 2 to 4 weeks of abstinence in several studies; slow-wave sleep recovering over months to years; fragmentation found up to one to two years after stopping.

evidence.extracted: As summarized: as alcohol use becomes chronic, alcohol has less of a hypnotic (sleep-promoting) effect; clinical insomnia in about 35 to 70% of alcohol users depending on the setting and stage of use, against about 15 to 30% in the general population; sleep complaints in alcohol use disorder are one of the most refractory problems to resolve, and insomnia is the most frequent complaint after stopping drinking.

evidence.locator: Alcohol › Objective measurements: Sleep latency, Total sleep time, Slow-wave sleep, Rapid eye movement and Objective sleep quality subsections
evidence.extracted: As summarized: alcohol can shorten sleep latency in healthy people; in alcohol use disorder sleep latency is prolonged during drinking and acute and post-acute withdrawal, total sleep time is reduced, slow-wave sleep deficits may take months to years to recover, REM rebounds after stopping with inconsistent findings, and sleep-stage switches are increased compared with healthy controls from the second night of abstinence to as long as one to two years.

evidence.locator: Alcohol › Relationship between subjective measurements and clinical outcomes, 1st paragraph; Relationship between objective measurements and clinical outcomes, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As summarized: self-reported insomnia during early abstinence predicted drinking or relapse in several studies; longer sleep latency in the first two weeks increased the odds of relapse in one study, longer sleep latency and lower sleep efficiency after 16 days and 19 weeks were associated with lower abstinence rates at 14 months in a second, and sleep latency at 5 days did not differ between later relapsers and abstainers in a third; slow-wave and REM measures gave mixed results.

Narrative, non-systematic review; Table 2 marks every early-abstinence alcohol cell as insufficient or conflicting data, while the text describes prolonged sleep latency and reduced total sleep in acute withdrawal.

risk_of_bias.note: Cited studies not appraisable through a narrative review.

inconsistency.note: REM findings conflict, as the claim says; the main directions are consistent as described.

indirectness.note: Second-hand figures from a narrative review.

grade.reasoning: Observational studies start low; rated down for risk of bias and indirectness because they are seen only through a narrative review (METHODS 6.3). Stays draft. Status replicated as described: several cited studies for each main direction.
